text:
Agallochon (Aloewood / Aquilaria) — Properties and Uses

Agallochon [aloewood]: an Indian wood, also known as agallochon or fragrant wood. It has warming properties and aids digestion; it strengthens the mouth and stomach, and when decocted in wine is beneficial for those suffering from liver ailments. When applied to the forehead together with rose oil [rhodinon], it relieves headache. When burned as incense, it produces a pleasant and aromatic fragrance.

Original: ἀγάλλοχον — Indian wood, also called agallochon or fragrant wood. It is warming, digestive, strengthens the mouth and stomach, is good for those with liver conditions when decocted in wine. Applied to the forehead with rose oil it helps headache. Burned as incense it is pleasant and aromatic.
title: Agallochon (Aloewood / Aquilaria) — Properties and Uses

text:
Wine of Maronea (Maron): Properties and Medicinal Uses

The wine of Maronea, which Homer mentions in the Odyssey as the wine Odysseus [Ulysses] gave to the Cyclops [Polyphemus]: it was of such great strength that it was diluted with twenty measures of water to one of wine. In its medicinal applications it warms the stomach, aids digestion [pepsis], promotes the flow of urine, and benefits those suffering from an excess of phlegm [phlegma]. In general, the stronger wines are the most warming and possess the greatest potency [dynamis].

Original: Maron (Wine of Maronea — Thrace) — The wine of Maronea mentioned in Homer's Odyssey when Odysseus gave it to the Cyclops. So strong that it was mixed with twenty measures of water to one of wine. Used medicinally: warms the stomach, promotes digestion, increases urine, helps those with phlegm. The strongest wines are most warming and have most power.
title: Wine of Maronea (Maron): Properties and Medicinal Uses

text:
Wormwood Wine (Absinthites Oinos)

Absinthites Oinos (Wormwood Wine) — ἀψινθίτης οἶνος: A medicinal wine prepared by steeping the leaves and flowers of wormwood in grape must [unfermented or partially fermented grape juice]. When taken as a drink, it warms the stomach and provides relief to those suffering from fluxes [diarrhea or dysentery] of the belly. It is also beneficial for those afflicted with jaundice, and for those who have been harmed by drinking hemlock. It is counted among the most widely prescribed of the medicinal wines.

Original: Absinthites Oinos (Wormwood Wine) — ἀψινθίτης οἶνος — Wormwood wine. Wormwood leaves and flowers steeped in grape must. Taken in drink it warms the stomach and helps those with fluxes of the belly. Good for those with jaundice and for those who have been made ill by drinking hemlock. One of the most widely prescribed medicinal wines.
title: Wormwood Wine (Absinthites Oinos)

text:
Squill Wine (Scillites Oinos)

Scillites Oinos [Squill Wine]: A wine prepared from sea squill [Urginea maritima]. It is administered for coughs and affections of the chest, for those suffering from chronic phlegm lodged in the chest, for dropsy [edema], and as a remedy against the bite of vipers. The preparation consists of steeping dried squill root in new wine [must] for a period of forty days.

Original: σκιλλίτης οἶνος — Squill wine made from sea squill (Urginea maritima). Given for coughs and chest conditions, for those with longstanding phlegm in the chest, for dropsy (edema), and for the bite of vipers. Prepared by soaking dried squill root in must for 40 days.
title: Squill Wine (Scillites Oinos)

text:
Rose Wine (Rhodites Oinos)

Rhodites Oinos [Rose Wine]: A wine prepared by macerating rose petals in unfermented grape juice [must] for the period of one year. It is of a cooler temperament than plain wine. It is beneficial for those suffering from ailments of the stomach, headache, and disorders of the mouth and gums. When applied externally to wounds, it reduces [cools] inflammation. It was the most widely prescribed medicinal wine in the Greek and Roman traditions, serving as a base vehicle for other medicinal preparations.

Original: Rhodites Oinos (Rose Wine) — ῥοδίτης οἶνος — Rose wine, made by macerating rose petals in must for one year. Cooler than plain wine. Good for those with stomach conditions, headache, and conditions of the mouth and gums. Applied to wounds it cools inflammation. The most widely prescribed medicinal wine in Greek/Roman tradition — rose wine as a base for other medicinal preparations.
title: Rose Wine (Rhodites Oinos)

text:
Oxymeli (Honey-Vinegar Preparation)

Oxymeli [honey-vinegar] — The best is prepared from vinegar and Attic honey boiled together. It is given to those suffering from coughs, to those with bilious conditions, and to those experiencing palpitations of the heart. Mixed with water, it purges the bowels. Applied externally, it brings relief to those with conditions of the joints [arthritis].

Original: ὀξύμελι — ὄξος καὶ μέλι Ἀττικὸν ἑψηθέντα. διδόμενον τοῖς βήττουσι, τοῖς χολώδεσι, τοῖς παλμοὺς ἔχουσι τῆς καρδίας. μετὰ ὕδατος κιρνάμενον τὴν κοιλίαν ὑπάγει. ἔξωθεν δὲ ἐπιτιθέμενον τοῖς ἀρθριτικοῖς βοηθεῖ.
title: Oxymeli (Honey-Vinegar Preparation)

text:
Melikraton (Hydromel / Mead): Honey-Water Preparation and Its Uses

Melikraton [hydromel / mead]: old water mixed with honey. The finest honey is dissolved in the purest water and reduced by boiling. When taken as a drink it is laxative, beneficial to those suffering from coughs, and clears the chest. When applied externally to wounds it cleanses them. It is also employed as a vehicle [base medium] for other medicinal plants.

Original: μελίκρατον — Old water mixed with honey. The best honey dissolves in the purest water and is boiled down. Taken in drink it is laxative, helps those with coughs, clears the chest. Applied to wounds it cleanses them. Used as a vehicle for other medicinal plants.
title: Melikraton (Hydromel / Mead): Honey-Water Preparation and Its Uses

text:
Bloodstone (Hematite) as a Mineral Medicine

The bloodstone [lithos haimatites]: Ground finely and taken as a drink with wine, it arrests fluxes of the belly and hemorrhage of the uterus. Applied to the eyes together with egg white, it diminishes inflammation. Ground finely and applied directly to wounds, it draws the edges [lips] of the wound together.

Original: λίθος αἱματίτης — Bloodstone (hematite, iron ore). Ground finely and taken in drink with wine it stops fluxes of the belly and uterine hemorrhage. Applied to the eyes with egg white it reduces inflammation. Ground finely and applied to wounds it draws the lips together.
title: Bloodstone (Hematite) as a Mineral Medicine

text:
Alum (Stypteria): Properties and Medical Uses

Alum [stypteria, στυπτηρία]: The finest variety is the rounded type [scholiasts identify this as 'round alum,' stromatites or sphairites] originating from Egypt. It possesses drawing [styptic], drying, and astringent qualities. When dissolved in warm water and used as a gargle, it is beneficial for affections of the mouth and tonsils. When applied directly to granulating [flesh-forming] wounds, it promotes their closure. Mixed with honey, it is applied to foul [putrid, κακοήθη] ulcers. Applied in vinegar to weeping [running, rheumatizing] sores, it brings about healing. It is among the most widely employed mineral antiseptics across all ancient medical traditions.

Original: Alum (Stypteria) — στυπτηρία — Alum. The best is the roundish kind from Egypt. It has drawing, drying, astringent properties. Dissolved in warm water and gargled it helps conditions of the mouth and tonsils. Applied to granulating wounds it helps them close. Mixed with honey it is applied to foul ulcers. Applied in vinegar to running sores it heals them. One of the most universally used mineral antiseptics across all ancient traditions.
title: Alum (Stypteria): Properties and Medical Uses

text:
Chrysokolla (Gold-Solder Mineral): Ophthalmic, Wound, and Emetic Uses

Chrysokolla [gold-solder]: the substance employed by goldsmiths. When applied to the eyes, it sharpens and clarifies the vision. When applied to wounds, it promotes their closure. When ingested with water, it is bitter in taste and induces vomiting.

Original: χρυσόκολλα — Gold-solder, the material used by goldsmiths. Applied to the eyes it clears the vision. Applied to wounds it helps them close. Taken with water it is bitter and causes vomiting.
title: Chrysokolla (Gold-Solder Mineral): Ophthalmic, Wound, and Emetic Uses

text:
White Poppy (Mekon Leuke) — Opium, Preparations, and Dosage

White Poppy [μήκων λευκή, mēkōn leukē]. The juice extracted from the heads, once dried, is called opion [ὄπιον]. It is of lesser potency than the black variety. The milky sap of the heads, taken as a drink, induces sleep. The seeds, taken together with wine and honey, promote sleep and arrest fluxes [discharges] of the belly. The heads boiled in water, with the resulting liquid applied externally to the forehead, relieves headache. Regarding dosage: a small amount is beneficial; a larger amount is fatal. [The entry continues with an extended discussion of the pharmacological gradations of opium, ranging from soporific to lethal effects.]

Original: μήκων λευκή — White poppy. The juice of the heads, dried, is called opion. Of lesser strength than the black kind. The milk from the heads taken in drink is soporific. The seeds taken with wine and honey provoke sleep and stop fluxes of the belly. The heads boiled in water and the liquid applied to the forehead stops headache. Note on dose: a little helps, more is lethal. Extended entry on the pharmacological gradations of opium from soporific to lethal.
title: White Poppy (Mekon Leuke) — Opium, Preparations, and Dosage

text:
Black Henbane (Hyoscyamus niger): Properties, Uses, and Antidotes

Black Henbane [hyoskyamos ho melas]: The leaves of all varieties, if taken in excessive quantity, produce madness and loss of rational faculty. The seed, drunk in wine, induces hallucinations [phantasiai] and deep sleep [koma]. Applied to the eyes together with woman's milk, it alleviates pain. The root, boiled in wine and held in the mouth, relieves toothache. ANTIDOTES: Should a person have consumed too much henbane, administer honeyed wine [oxymel] or a decoction of radish in water, so as to provoke vomiting and expel the substance.

Original: ὑοσκύαμος ὁ μέλας — The leaves of all kinds, taken in excess, cause madness and loss of reason. The seed drunk in wine causes hallucinations and deep sleep. Applied to the eyes with woman's milk it relieves pain. The root boiled in wine and held in the mouth relieves toothache. ANTIDOTES: If someone has drunk too much henbane, give them honeyed wine (oxymel) or decoction of radish in water to vomit it out.
title: Black Henbane (Hyoscyamus niger): Properties, Uses, and Antidotes

text:
Mandrake: Toxic and Therapeutic Properties, Including Surgical Anaesthesia

Mandragoras [Mandrake]. The root, beaten together with olive oil and applied as a poultice, is beneficial for wounds rendered frostbitten. Boiled in wine and applied externally, it aids those suffering from gout, diseases of the joints, and those afflicted by erysipelas [a streptococcal skin infection]. Preparation of the root as a medicinal wine: take one mina [c. 431 g] of root to one amphora [c. 26 litres] of must [unfermented grape juice], and allow to stand for three months. This preparation is given prior to surgical operations and cauterisations in order to produce insensibility to pain [analgesia/anaesthesia]. Those who drink in excess of the proper measure are rendered mute [or: speechless] permanently.

Original: μανδραγόρας — Mandrake. The root beaten with olive oil and applied is good for wounds that have been made frostbitten. Boiled in wine and applied it helps those with gout, with conditions of the joints, and those bitten by erysipelas. The root prepared as a wine: take one mina of root to one amphora of must, let stand for three months. Given before operations and cauterisations to produce insensibility to pain. Those who drink more than the due measure are made speechless forever.
title: Mandrake: Toxic and Therapeutic Properties, Including Surgical Anaesthesia

text:
Hemlock (Konion): Topical and Toxic Uses, Antidote, and Historical Note

Konion [κώνειον, Hemlock]: The entire plant is cold in quality and narcotic [narkōtikon] in effect. The juice of the plant, applied to the testicles before the onset of puberty, prevents their growth and suppresses sexual desire. Likewise, applied to the breasts of girls before they have developed, it arrests breast growth. The physicians of earlier times employed hemlock for this purpose — to prevent excessive development of the breasts. However, if hemlock is taken internally as a drink, it is fatal. It kills by chilling the body progressively from the lower parts upward, until the cold reaches the heart and lungs. ANTIDOTE: Administer warm wine and compel the patient to walk; if sleep threatens to overcome them, keep them awake by every possible means. [Translator's historical note: The death of Socrates in 399 BCE, as recounted by Plato in the Phaedo, corresponds precisely with Dioscorides' account of hemlock poisoning — a numbness and coldness ascending from the feet toward the heart.]

Original: Konion (Hemlock — Socrates' poison) — κώνειον — Hemlock. The whole plant is cold and narcotic. The juice of the plant applied to the testicles before puberty prevents them from growing and stops desire. Applied to the breasts of girls before they develop it prevents the breasts from growing. The ancient physicians used hemlock to prevent excessive breast development. But taken in drink hemlock kills. It kills by making the body cold from below upward until it reaches the heart and lungs. ANTIDOTE: Give warm wine and make the patient walk until sleep overcomes them — keep them awake if possible. Historical note: The death of Socrates (399 BCE) as described by Plato in the Phaedo matches Dioscorides' description of hemlock poisoning exactly — numbness ascending from feet to heart.
title: Hemlock (Konion): Topical and Toxic Uses, Antidote, and Historical Note

text:
Aconite (Wolfsbane): Toxicity and Antidotes

Akoníton [ἀκόνιτον] — Aconite (wolfsbane). Of all things, this plant kills most swiftly. It kills by inducing a sensation of chilling [i.e., by cooling the vital heat]. When smeared upon meat and given to leopards and wild beasts, it kills them quickly — from which it derives its name 'leopard's bane' [pardaliankhes]. ANTIDOTE: Castor oil [kiki] administered immediately, or wine mixed with myrrh, or raisin wine [passum] combined with absinthium [wormwood], or a decoction of wormwood. If any of these remedies is administered promptly, the patient may be preserved.

Original: Akonition (Aconite / Wolfsbane) — ἀκόνιτον — Aconite (wolfsbane). This plant is of all things the swiftest to kill. It kills by chilling. Given to leopards and wild beasts smeared on meat it kills them quickly — hence it is called leopard's bane. ANTIDOTE: Castor oil taken immediately, or wine and myrrh, or raisin wine with absinthium, or wormwood decoction. If these are given quickly the patient is saved.
title: Aconite (Wolfsbane): Toxicity and Antidotes

text:
Strychnos (Nightshade): Three Kinds and Their Pharmacological Gradations

Strychnos [στρύχνος, 'nightshade']: Dioscorides documents three distinct kinds. (1) The garden kind [στρύχνος κηπαῖος]: identified with Solanum nigrum; described as soporific [sleep-inducing] but comparatively less dangerous. (2) The mad kind [στρύχνος μανικός]: possibly Datura or Atropa belladonna; causes madness [delirium] and hallucinations. (3) The killing kind [στρύχνος ὑπνωτικός or equivalent]: identified with Atropa belladonna or Hyoscyamus niger; lethal when taken in excess. The plant family Solanaceae — encompassing henbane [Hyoscyamus], mandrake [Mandragora], belladonna [Atropa], Datura, and Solanum — yielded a greater number of pharmaceutical compounds than any other plant family represented in this archive. Dioscorides' tripartite classification of nightshade constitutes the earliest systematic effort to differentiate pharmacological gradations within a toxic plant genus.

Original: Strychnos (Nightshade family) — στρύχνος — Nightshade (multiple species). Three kinds documented by Dioscorides: (1) the garden kind (Solanum nigrum) — soporific but not as dangerous; (2) the mad kind (possibly Datura or belladonna) — causes madness and hallucinations; (3) the killing kind (Atropa belladonna or Hyoscyamus) — lethal in excess. The Solanaceae family — henbane, mandrake, belladonna, Datura, Solanum — produced more pharmaceutical compounds than any other plant family in the archive. Dioscorides' classification of three kinds of nightshade represents the first systematic attempt to distinguish the pharmacological gradations within a toxic plant genus.
title: Strychnos (Nightshade): Three Kinds and Their Pharmacological Gradations

text:
General Principles of Antidote Treatment (Book VI closing section)

Antidotes [ἀντίδοτα] — General Principles. Dioscorides concludes Book VI with the following foundational principles of antidote treatment: (1) Emetics are to be administered first, so as to expel the poison swiftly from the body; (2) Warm wine is to be given following the emetic, as it counteracts and warms poisons that are cold in nature; (3) Treatment must be applied in opposition to the action of the poison — cold poisons are to be treated with warmth, and hot poisons with cooling agents; (4) The patient is to be kept in motion, as movement delays the absorption of certain poisons into the body. These principles anticipate the approach of modern toxicology: decontamination, the administration of antidotes, and supportive care. The Greek and Roman development of systematic toxicology — represented by Nicander of Colophon (2nd century BCE) and Dioscorides (77 CE) — constitutes the first systematic body of pharmacological science.

Original: ἀντίδοτα — Antidotes and their general principles. (1) Emetics first — get the poison out quickly; (2) Warm wine given after emetic — warms the cold poisons; (3) Opposite treatment to the poison's action — cold poisons treated with warmth; hot poisons with cooling; (4) Movement — keeping the patient active delays absorption of some poisons.
title: General Principles of Antidote Treatment (Book VI closing section)

text:
On Pepper: Properties, Uses, and Adulteration Test

From De Materia Medica by Pedanius Dioscorides (77 CE), Book I. On Pepper (Greek: κόσκινον; Latin: Piper nigrum and Piper longum). Both varieties of pepper possess warming [calorific], diuretic, and digestive [peptic] properties. They dissolve and expel intestinal flatulence, and are of benefit to those suffering from chills and shivering fits. When rubbed upon the eyelids, they sharpen the eyesight; they draw down [attract] moisture from the head; and when administered in wine, they are prescribed for tetanus [opisthotonos] and epilepsy [the falling sickness]. When applied together with honey, they disperse opacity [leucoma] of the cornea. Long pepper [Piper longum] is more heating in its action than round pepper [Piper nigrum]. Adulteration of pepper may be identified by means of water: genuine pepper sinks to the bottom, while adulterated pepper floats on the surface. Preparation: administered internally in wine or mixed with honey; applied topically to the eyes. Conditions treated: digestive complaints, intestinal gas, chills, tetanus, epilepsy, corneal film [leucoma], and head congestion.

Original: De Materia Medica, Pedanius Dioscorides (77 CE), Book I. On Pepper (κόσκινον / Piper nigrum, P. longum). 'Both kinds of pepper are warming, diuretic, and digestive. They break up intestinal gas, are beneficial for those chilled and shivering, clear the eyesight when rubbed on eyelids, attract moisture from the head, and are given for tetanus and epilepsy in wine. Applied with honey they clear corneal film. The long pepper is more warming than the round. Adulterated pepper may be detected by water — true pepper sinks, adulterated floats.' Preparation: taken in wine or honey, applied topically to eyes. Conditions: digestive complaints, chills, tetanus, eye conditions, head congestion.
title: On Pepper: Properties, Uses, and Adulteration Test

text:
On Iris: Properties and Medical Uses

On Iris (ἶρις). The root is warming [calorific], sharp [acrid], and somewhat bitter in quality. It softens tissue and draws out embedded splinters; when applied topically with vinegar, it disperses hard swellings beneath the chin [scrofulous or glandular swellings]. When taken internally in wine, it relieves pain in the sides, convulsions, ruptures [hernias], coughs, and inflammation of the trachea [windpipe]. Mixed with honey and applied to the head, it cures dandruff [scurf of the scalp]. When applied as a pessary [vaginal suppository], it promotes the menstrual flux and expels the afterbirth [placenta]. The smoke [of the burnt root] drives away serpents.

Original: De Materia Medica, Book I. On Iris (ἶρις). The root is warming, sharp, and somewhat bitter. It softens and draws out splinters, and being applied with vinegar it disperses hard swellings under the chin. Taken in wine it relieves pain of the sides, convulsions, ruptures, coughs, and inflammation of the trachea. With honey applied to the head it cures dandruff. Applied as a pessary it moves the menstrual flux and expels the afterbirth. The smoke drives away serpents.
title: On Iris: Properties and Medical Uses

text:
On Nard: Celtic and Indian Varieties (Dioscorides, De Materia Medica I.12)

Nard [Nardus] is warming and drying. It is beneficial to the stomach, arrests diarrhea, promotes urination, and applied in oil is good for the head. It benefits the liver and kidneys, and is of service to those suffering from jaundice. Given in wine with pepper, it aids those bitten by serpents. Applied to the eyes with raisin wine [passum], it removes inflammation. The Indian kind is stronger than the Celtic.

Original: Nardus calefacit et siccat, stomachi utilis est, diarrhoeam sistit, urinam ciet, et ex oleo capiti prodest. Hepar et renes iuvat, ictericis auxiliatur. In vino cum pipere haustum serpentium morsis medetur. Cum vino uvae passae oculis admotum inflammationes tollit. Indica Celtica validior est.
title: On Nard: Celtic and Indian Varieties (Dioscorides, De Materia Medica I.12)

text:
On Costus: Properties, Uses, and Preparations

Costus [Κόστος] is warming and drying in quality. When taken as a drink, it benefits those who have been bitten by serpents and those suffering from pain in the side. It stimulates the menstrual flow, promotes urination, aids those afflicted with dropsy [edema], and alleviates epilepsy. Taken with wine, it acts against poisons. When applied topically with honey, it removes dark blotches and spots from the skin. The root, when burned as incense, repels serpents. The Arabian variety is considered the finest, followed by the Indian.

Original: Costus is warming and drying. Taken in drink it helps those bitten by serpents and those with pain in the side. It moves the menstrual flux, provokes urine, helps those with dropsy, and eases epilepsy. Taken with wine it helps against poisons. Applied with honey it removes dark blotches and spots. The root burned as incense drives away serpents. The Arabian kind is best, then the Indian.
title: On Costus: Properties, Uses, and Preparations

text:
On Poppy Juice and Opium (De Materia Medica, Book II, Chapter 76)

From De Materia Medica, Book II, concerning the juice of the poppy [opium] (Greek: ὀπός μήκωνος; Latin botanical: Papaver somniferum): 'The juice of the wild poppy is the most potent of all sleep-inducing substances [soporifics]. It relieves pain, brings on sleep, promotes digestion, and is beneficial for coughs and for the spitting of blood. Taken as a drink, it is of service to those suffering from chronic ailments and from pains of the intestines. However, when used in excess it is harmful, for it renders men torpid and brings about death. Genuine opium may be recognized by its bitterness and by the swiftness with which it weighs heavily upon the senses. That which has been adulterated is less bitter and correspondingly less effective.' Method of preparation: the dried latex is dissolved in wine or water. Conditions treated: pain, insomnia, cough, intestinal pain. Editorial note: Dioscorides explicitly cautions against lethal overdose, representing the earliest documented pharmacological warning regarding opioid substances in the Western medical tradition.

Original: De Materia Medica, Book II. On Poppy Juice/Opium (ὀπός μήκωνος / Papaver somniferum). 'The juice of the wild poppy is the most powerful of the soporifics. It eases pain, induces sleep, aids digestion, is good for coughs and for spitting blood. Taken in drink it benefits those with chronic illnesses and with intestinal pains. But used too much it harms, for it makes men lethargic and kills them. One may know the genuine by its bitterness and by its rapid heaviness upon the senses. The adulterated is less bitter and less effective.' Preparation: dried latex dissolved in wine or water. Conditions: pain, insomnia, cough, intestinal pain. Critical note: Dioscorides explicitly warns of lethal overdose — the first documented pharmacological warning about opioids in Western medicine.
title: On Poppy Juice and Opium (De Materia Medica, Book II, Chapter 76)

text:
On the Willow: Medicinal Uses of Leaves and Bark

From De Materia Medica, Book II, on the Willow (Greek: ἰτέα; Latin: Salix species): The leaves and bark of the willow, boiled together with a small amount of pepper and drunk, arrest looseness of the bowels [flux of the belly, i.e., diarrhea]. The juice extracted by pressing the leaves, when dropped into the ears, relieves pain within them. The bark, when burned and dissolved in vinegar, removes corns and calluses [indurated skin growths]. The leaves, finely bruised and taken with a little pepper and wine, suppress involuntary seminal emission [flowing of the seed] in those afflicted by nocturnal dreams [wet dreams]. The bark of the willow, when boiled and the resulting decoction drunk, provides relief to those suffering from gout. Preparation methods include: boiling leaves in water; preparing a decoction of bark; and bruising leaves for internal use. Conditions addressed: diarrhea, otalgia [ear pain], hyperkeratosis [corns and calluses], spermatorrhea [involuntary seminal emission], and gout [podagra].

Original: De Materia Medica, Book II. On Willow (ἰτέα / Salix species). 'The leaves and bark of the willow, being boiled with a little pepper and drunk, they stop the flux of the belly. The juice pressed from the leaves being dropped into the ears stops the pain in them. The bark burned and dissolved in vinegar removes corns and calluses. The leaves bruised small and taken with a little pepper and wine stop the flowing of the seed in those troubled by dreams. The bark of the willow being boiled and the decoction drunk helps those troubled with gout.' Preparation: leaves boiled in water; bark decocted; leaves bruised. Conditions: diarrhea, ear pain, gout, skin conditions.
title: On the Willow: Medicinal Uses of Leaves and Bark

text:
Wheat and Grain Medicines: Therapeutic Uses of Triticum

From De Materia Medica, Book III. Concerning Wheat and Grain-Based Medicines (Greek: πυρός [pyros]; Latin: Triticum, and related grains). 'Wheat flour, applied as a poultice together with boiled figs, softens [mollifies] and brings to maturation [ripens] swellings. Bread crumbs, chewed and then applied to the skin, draw out splinters. The water in which wheat has been boiled is beneficial for the throat when used as a gargle. A decoction [boiled extract] of green [unripe] wheat, applied to the temples with oil, relieves headache. Old lard rendered [melted down and clarified] together with wheat flour and applied warm relieves pain of the joints, and is of benefit to those suffering from gout and sciatica.' Methods of preparation include: flour poultice, topical application of chewed bread, and decoctions. Conditions treated: swellings, embedded splinters, sore throat, headache, and joint pain (including gout and sciatica).

Original: De Materia Medica, Book III. On Wheat and Grain Medicines (πυρός / Triticum and related). 'The flour of wheat applied in a poultice with boiled figs mollifies and ripens swellings. Bread crumbs chewed and applied draw out splinters. The water in which wheat has been boiled is good for the throat when gargled. The decoction of green wheat applied with oil to the temples eases headache. Old lard rendered with wheat flour applied warm relieves pain of the joints and helps those with gout and sciatica.' Preparation: flour poultice; bread applied; decoctions. Conditions: swellings, splinters, sore throat, headache, joint pain.
title: Wheat and Grain Medicines: Therapeutic Uses of Triticum

text:
On Saffron (Crocus sativus) — De Materia Medica, Book III, Chapter 25

De Materia Medica, Book III. Concerning Saffron [κρόκος / Crocus sativus]. Saffron possesses a warming, softening, and sleep-inducing property [faculty]. It is beneficial to the eyes and to the stomach. When taken as a drink, it sharpens the eyesight. When applied topically with honey and wine to sites of inflammation, it affords relief. When taken in wine as a drink, it gladdens [cheers] the mind. Administered with wine, it assists those who have been bitten by the land-crocodile [a terrestrial reptile, likely a large lizard or monitor]. Applied as a pessary [vaginal suppository], it promotes [moves] the menstrual flow. However, when consumed in excess, it is harmful, producing a form of intoxication.

Original: De Materia Medica, Book III. On Saffron/Crocus (κρόκος / Crocus sativus). 'Saffron has a warming, softening, and sleep-inducing faculty. It benefits the eyes and the stomach. Taken in drink it sharpens the sight. Applied with honey and wine to inflammations it helps them. Taken with wine in drink it cheers the mind. Given with wine it helps those bitten by the land-crocodile. Applied as a pessary it moves the menstrual flux. But taken in excess it harms by inducing a kind of intoxication.'
title: On Saffron (Crocus sativus) — De Materia Medica, Book III, Chapter 25

text:
On Aloe: Properties, Preparations, and Conditions Treated

De Materia Medica, Book III. Concerning Aloe (Greek: ἀλόη; Aloe vera and related species). Aloe possesses astringent [binding] properties and is moderately bitter in taste. When applied topically, it arrests bleeding from wounds, draws wounds closed, and is beneficial for the eyes. When consumed as a drink, it loosens the bowels and purges bile [acts as a cholagogue]. Applied to the scalp together with wine and oil, it removes dandruff [furfur capitis] and arrests hair loss. When applied warm, it heals hemorrhoids [haemorrhoids]. The finest variety is that known as the Barbarian kind, which is transparent in appearance, resembling glass, and of a saffron [crocus] color.

Original: De Materia Medica, Book III. On Aloe (ἀλόη / Aloe vera and related species). 'Aloe has the property of binding and is somewhat bitter. It stops bleeding from wounds when applied, closes together wounds, and is good for the eyes. Taken in drink it loosens the belly and purges bile. Applied to the head with wine and oil it clears dandruff. It stops the falling off of hair. Applied warm it heals the haemorrhoids. The best is the Barbarian kind, which is transparent like glass and saffron-coloured.'
title: On Aloe: Properties, Preparations, and Conditions Treated

text:
Dioscorides on Mandrake: Properties, Preparations, and Uses

From De Materia Medica, Book IV. Concerning Mandrake (Greek: μανδραγόρας; Mandragora officinarum). 'The root possesses a warming quality. Wine prepared from the root, when drunk in the measure of one cyathus [a small cup-measure, approximately 45 ml], induces sleep [acts as a soporific] in those who must undergo cutting or cauterization, so that they may not feel the pain. It is likewise given as a drink to those suffering from serpent-bites, and administered to those who have swallowed the juice of aconite [serving as an antidote to that poison]. When applied as a pessary [vaginal suppository], it stimulates the menstrual flow. The bark and root, when applied with oil, heal inflammation and prurigo [itching skin conditions]. However, an excessive dose brings on lethargy and may even cause death.' Preparation: the root steeped in wine and drunk as a surgical anesthetic; also applied topically with oil. Conditions treated: surgical anesthesia, snakebite, aconite poisoning, menstrual irregularity, inflammation, prurigo. Historical note: this passage represents the earliest documented description of surgical anesthesia in the European medical tradition, predating the use of ether by approximately 1,800 years.

Original: De Materia Medica, Book IV. On Mandrake (μανδραγόρας / Mandragora officinarum). 'The root has the quality of warming. Wine made of the root, a cyathus [small measure] being drunk, is a soporific for those who need to be cut or cauterized, that they may not feel the pain. Given in drink to those with serpent-bites, and in drink for those who drink the juice of aconite [poison antidote]. Applied as a pessary it moves the menstrual flux. The bark and root applied with oil heals inflammation and prurigo. But excess causes lethargy and even death.' Preparation: root in wine as surgical anesthetic; applied topically. Conditions: surgical anesthesia, snakebite, menstrual disorders. Note: earliest documented description of surgical anesthesia in European medicine — 1,800 years before ether.
title: Dioscorides on Mandrake: Properties, Preparations, and Uses

text:
On Stramonium / Thorn Apple: Doses, Toxicity, and Therapeutic Uses

From De Materia Medica, Book IV. Concerning Stramonium, or Thorn Apple [στράμμωνον; Datura species]: When the root is drunk in wine, it causes the mind to wander. A single drachm [drachma] in weight produces visions of an extraordinary nature; two drachms induce madness lasting three days; four drachms prove fatal. The antidote is pine resin [resina pini] taken in wine. Applied externally with vinegar, it is beneficial for skin diseases and abscesses. The seed, worn around the neck as an amulet [amuletum], is said to be of service against epilepsy — though Dioscorides notes this may be mere superstition. Preparation: the root administered in wine in carefully measured small doses to produce visionary effects; also prepared as a topical application. Conditions treated: surgical anesthesia [narcosis], visionary or altered states, epilepsy. Editorial note: Dioscorides here records both the therapeutic and the lethal effects of Datura at differing doses, representing a notably sophisticated dose-response observation for the period.

Original: De Materia Medica, Book IV. On Stramonium/Thorn Apple (στράμμωνον / Datura species). 'The root being drunk in wine makes the mind wander — a drachm weight makes one have a vision beyond the ordinary, two drachms bring on madness for three days, four drachms kill. The antidote is pine resin drunk in wine. Applied topically with vinegar it is good for skin diseases and abscesses. The seed hung around the neck as an amulet helps against epilepsy — but this may be superstition.' Preparation: root in wine in precise small doses for vision; topical application. Conditions: surgical anesthesia, vision, epilepsy. Note: Dioscorides documents both the therapeutic and toxic effects of Datura at different doses — a sophisticated dose-response observation.
title: On Stramonium / Thorn Apple: Doses, Toxicity, and Therapeutic Uses

text:
On Honey: Properties, Uses, and Preparations (Dioscorides, De Materia Medica, Book V, Chapter 2)

From De Materia Medica, Book V: On Honey (Greek: μέλι; produced by Apis mellifera). Honey, when boiled and applied to old [chronic] wounds, draws out their contents, cleanses them, and promotes the growth of new flesh [granulation]. When taken with water, it clears the chest and lungs and loosens [expectoration of] cough. It aids digestion and expels whatever burdens the stomach. Attic honey [from the region of Attica, Greece] is most highly esteemed — it is dry in quality and does not putrefy. Applied to the teeth and gums, it firms up loose teeth. Rubbed on the eyelids, it disperses dimness [opacity or obscuration] before the eyes. The worst kinds of honey are those derived from box trees [Buxus sempervirens] and yew [Taxus baccata], as these produce nausea and vomiting. Preparations: applied directly and warm to wounds; taken internally mixed with water [hydromel]; rubbed onto teeth, gums, and eyelids. Conditions treated: chronic wounds, respiratory ailments (chest congestion, cough), digestive complaints, eye conditions (dimness of vision), dental looseness.

Original: De Materia Medica, Book V. On Honey (μέλι / Apis mellifera product). 'Honey, being boiled and applied to old wounds, draws out what is in them and cleanses them and produces flesh. Taken with water it clears the chest and lungs and loosens the cough. It digests and expels what burdens the stomach. Attic honey is the most praised — it is dry and does not rot. Applied to the teeth and gums it fastens loose teeth. Rubbed on the eyelids it removes the darkness before the eyes. The worst honey is that from box trees and yew — it produces nausea and vomiting.' Preparation: applied directly to wounds; taken with water; rubbed on teeth and eyes. Conditions: wounds, respiratory, digestive, eye conditions, dental.
title: On Honey: Properties, Uses, and Preparations (Dioscorides, De Materia Medica, Book V, Chapter 2)

text:
Copper and Verdigris: Medicinal Uses (Dioscorides, De Materia Medica, Book V)

The flower of copper [verdigris, i.e., basic copper acetate or copper carbonate patina] being applied stops the flow of blood from wounds and cleanses foul ulcers. When applied with honey, it draws together the edges of wounds. Used as an eye salve, it sharpens the sight. Beaten fine and applied, it arrests excessive menstrual flow. Washed copper [i.e., copper that has been rinsed or purified] applied with vinegar removes eruptions of the skin and dandruff. Copper vessels used for water storage prevent the water from putrefying.

Original: The flower of copper [verdigris] being applied stops the flows of blood from wounds and cleanses foul ulcers. Applied with honey it draws together the edges of wounds. Used as an eye salve it sharpens the sight. Beaten fine and applied it stops excessive menstrual flow. Washed copper applied with vinegar removes eruptions of the skin and dandruff. Copper vessels for water storage keep the water from putrefying.
title: Copper and Verdigris: Medicinal Uses (Dioscorides, De Materia Medica, Book V)
